newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia may defer projects, won't prop up ringgit.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia may defer projects, won't prop up ringgit.

text.p: Malaysia may defer some big import items and less important infrastructure projects to cushion the impact of a weak ringgit on the trade account, Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said on Tuesday.

Speaking to reporters after visiting the site of the country's new international airport in the town of Sepang, Anwar also reiterated that the government would not intervene to support the falling ringgit.
The government would review projects that have not yet started and were not considered "critical" or strategic to Malaysia, the national news agency Bernama quoted him as saying.
"There will be an impact if nothing is done," Anwar said.

Projects like the Kuala Lumpur International Airport and sea ports were among those considered strategic, but "there are maybe some projects which we think we can defer", Bernama quoted him as saying.
The government was also looking at how to reduce the import bill, which would likely escalate much more than expected due to the weaker ringgit.
"Therefore, we will have to look at other measures that include deferring lumpy items," Anwar said.

Malaysia was expected to have a trade deficit this year of 1.65 billion ringgit ($597 million) against a deficit of 619 million last year. The deficit in the first six months of the year was 2.7 billion ringgit against a deficit of 687.8 million in the same period last year.

The Malaysian unit has fallen almost 12 percent against the dollar in the last month. It fell two percent on Friday alone after Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said he was satisfied with the ringgit's level and said the central bank would not waste its reserves trying to defend the currency.
"We will look at the strength of the market and the... ringgit based on the strength of the economy," Bernama quoted Anwar as saying.
"The question of intervention does not arise."

Anwar, who is also finance minister, said he believed that with the country's strong economic fundamentals and impressive performance of Malaysian companies, foreign investors who had been withdrawing from the local capital market would return.
The ringgit hit a low of 2.7930 to a dollar early on Tuesday, its weakest level since February 1994, before rebounding to 2.7645/75 at 1000 GMT.
Anwar said that whatever moves the government made would be influenced by decisions and developments affecting the region.
He said the $16 billion package to rescue Thailand's economy could have a positive impact on regional currencies.
"We have to understand that negative reports on the region in general were triggered from Thailand," Anwar said.
At a meeting between the International Monetary Fund and other creditors on a bail-out package at a Tokyo meeting on Monday, the IMF and Japan agreed to contribute $4 billion each.

Australia, Hong Kong, Malaysia and Singapore pledged to contribute $1 billion each, South Korea and Indonesia $500 million each. Some $3 billion is expected to come from the World Bank, the Asian Development Bank and possibly China.
